utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, your Excellencies. [In English] Welcome, Judge Lattanzi. We are glad you are back with us. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me, Witness? Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you hear me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you also hear Mr. Karadzic's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when your column split and into how many columns?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Bornica, we split into three separate columns. And we went in three different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you and when was that, on what day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just noticed there was a bundles of papers open on the witness's desk, and I just wanted to clarify exactly what they were and if the witness is referring to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, could you tell us what documents you are looking at at the moment? Or you have with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an exhibit from the ground, and it is not a problem at all, I'll remove every single piece of paper from the desk so your wishes shall be granted in that respect as well. Here you are, no more papers, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To refresh your memory, if you need to take a look at one of those documents, please let us know. There should be no problem. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you think that the Trial Chamber may wish to see the papers, we can ask for that. When did those columns split, on what day?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the evening on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And those columns, did they communicate to each other, and if that was the case, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, everybody, forgive me, Your Honours, Judges. Can you be please -- can you explain how we communicated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please be asked not to overlap and wait for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I seem to be the culprit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You answered one part of my question. The second part of my question is this: Did you have physical contact? Did you open fire at each other during that first night and in what part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure he answered one part of your question at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpretation was not finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, ignore everything. Could you ask your question again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did those three columns communicate with each other? How did they inform each other of things?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had military Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the VRS listen to your conversations?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't tell you. I know nothing about that. I don't know whether the VRS listened to us. We had an encounter with the VRS at Kaldrmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about that yesterday. Did you get close to each other during that first night when those three columns moved about?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we passed the first Serbian line at Kaldrmica, between Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, one group passed and one group went in the direction of Tumaci [phoen] hill. The other group went in the direction of Cerska. From Kaldrmica to the school, there is a part there and the third group, Zulfo Tursun's group, arrived from the third side from Nova Kasaba. They had to by-pass a hill. When we arrived, when one part of the column arrived at Odaca [phoen], that night we were informed that there were problems and that the Serbs had set out from Kaldrmica to cut off Zulfo Tursun's army and that with his troops he would not be able to get to Udrc. And then one group separated, about 200 of us men, to assist them in order to protect Zulfo Tursun and his troops. We came down from Udrc towards one part of Cerska, between the two hill tops, and when we arrived there, we formed a line there, some 200 of us. We formed a line and we had contact with Zulfo Tursun who was from the other side of that hill so we met with him. We joined up with him. In the meantime, as for the Serbs coming from down there and shooting, Zulfo Tursun and ourselves accompanied by the late Ejub Golic deployed. We met those people, some 130 to 150 metres away from us. They were shooting and we shot back at them. It was only in the morning that we saw what we had done, Ibro Duda was killed, some of the troops of his were also killed, and some of the people. We managed to collect the weapons and the ammunition and we swore to each other that we would never tell anybody who we had killed and how we had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to you, how many people died there?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to me, a lot of people died there. I don't know how to explain. Maybe 500 to 600 people, even that would be too few, but let's say it was between 450 and 500 people altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, did you know anything about incidents in Srebrenica before you left? Were there any casualties there as a result of shelling and could you observe those happenings?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to explain to me whether you're talking about that case when I was deceived by Mladjo and Cvrk, and Cvrk was the goalkeeper. Is that about the killing of the children by shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that was all about?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that happened, a few days before that, a dispatch arrived at the Independent Mountain Battalion in Glogova, and in that dispatch Mevludin Zukic, who could read the dispatch, arrived from Sarajevo from Izetbegovic personally, that we had to protect ourselves because there would be fire. That meant that there would be an attack on Srebrenica and that we had to do something urgently in order to transport the people or that those people from NATO who were supposed to come to Srebrenica to help us, to protect us, that's how we were supposed to defend ourselves. And then a game was played, a tournament was organised in the football pitch, and children were playing. I was not on duty at that time. I don't know whether Mladjo asked for help from Ejub Golic. I suppose that the commanders knew what would happen, I went with a man called Cvrk from Zvolica [phoen]. I went to help them and in the courtroom in Srebrenica, there was something in the bags, I didn't know what that was, and when I arrived on the scene and when -- there was the 120-millimetre mortar that had fired that shell. We arrived there. When we arrived there I saw that, or rather, I thought that they would open fire on Bratunac or Ljubovija or perhaps some town in Serbia. And then my Mladjo told me that I was free to go. I arrived almost to the command of the Independent Mountain Battalion. That shell was fired from up there. And a few minutes later, people started running from the football pitch, from the school, towards the centre of Srebrenica where our command was. What happened, everybody was asking. And somebody said Chetniks shelled the football pitch and some children got killed. All of a sudden, everybody started saying that it was done by Chetniks, by the Serbs. It was ascribed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in Srebrenica itself, what was being said about the incident?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica itself, nothing was being said. What was being said was two days later when I went to the front line, I was on the front line, with my colleagues and we discussed that whole matter. The story was learned in Srebrenica a few days later when I came back to Srebrenica, and I lived in Srebrenica at the time. Can I mention the name of the place where I lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to me and said that I had to go to an interview. I was taken to the garbage depot. I didn't know where they were taking me until one group of guards from the Independent Battalion at Glogova was returning and they asked them where are you taking? They told them and they started to defend me. They returned me and I suppose that, like many others before me, I was supposed to be liquidated in that garbage depot, and then I was detained in the department store. I was there for a couple of days. I was detained. And then the late Ejub Golic arrived, took me to the command and told me not to tell anybody about that because it was all over but we shouldn't be talking about that to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 19 -- as far as I can remember, I believe that it was in 1995, two or three months before the attack on Srebrenica, thereabouts. Because the attack on Srebrenica was launched very soon after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us in view of your closeness to Oric and others, what was the objective of the BiH, or rather, those few commanders in Hornje [phoen]? What was their strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I explain to you, Mr. President and Judges, what the objective was? We knew what the objective of Naser Oric was and those people in Srebrenica who were closer to him. Their objective was to defend Srebrenica. People were supposed to defend Srebrenica and the others were supposed to get rich. Why? The humanitarian aid, when it arrived, we would be waiting for humanitarian aid for seven or 15 days for it to be distributed but before that, it was taken to the marketplace and it was sold there it by Naser's people and we were left with the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what were the intentions with regard to the Serbian territories and the Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you immediately that I did not understand your question at all. I don't know how to explain that to you. From the very beginning of the war, the intention was every Serb wanted to live in their own land, they didn't want to leave, and now what happened there, how did it change overnight, I really can't tell you. We -- I apologise for interrupting myself. All of us who knew each other, be it a Serb or a Muslim, we all wanted to live together. And then an operation happened and we saw each other in that operation. We called out each other's names but Naser Oric did not want us to socialise. He didn't want us to communicate with anybody. And people who wanted to talk to each other would be either killed or put into prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, and to what extent was there a connection or influence of Sarajevo over developments there and to what extent did Oric himself do that? You explained this about the shell a moment ago. What was the influence of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judges, already in 1993, from Sarajevo, either from Izetbegovic personally or whoever, we got something in writing. How do I put this? And you displayed that here in one case when Naser Oric was talking at this youth centre in Srebrenica where there is a disco-club now, he's talking about this conversation. In 1993, we got this offer to reach an agreement so as to leave Srebrenica which was offered for some parts near Sarajevo, Ilijas, Vogosca, Blazuj, and that had started, as far as I remember, in 1993. UNPROFOR people came with helicopters to get the army and the wounded out. And Swedish trucks took people out. This went on for seven days until that ambush of Zulfo Tursun and Naser on the yellow bridge, and then he came and said the Chetniks ambushed the people. But people were leaving for seven nights and seven days and the Serbs let us go, they went to Tuzla, they went through Bratunac and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the motive Oric's motive, to prevent the people from leaving?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his motive was because we figured all of that out until 1995, until the attack, how to explain this to you, Mr. President? That there was not a single military force, no force could have gone through the line that we held in 1995. He wanted to make as much money as possible to keep Srebrenica, to have decorations so the people would say Naser Oric did this, Naser Oric did that. As far as I know, Naser Oric was not tried here for the killing of some Muslims already in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Izetbegovic and his instructions. Did you personally have some experience with Izetbegovic, the president, and his son?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997, yes, I did meet with Alija Izetbegovic, when an offer was made to me. That lady colleague of yours who was in power and the Red Cross from Geneva, you and everybody, the Judges, have these documents, when I was freed because of this false killing, and I was amnestied on the basis of that paper, and I was exchanged for that captain that we mentioned a bit yesterday. And then Alija Izetbegovic gave me -- I had that little military booklet, and there is also this certificate with my name and surname stating how much money we as military had received, and he paid me in cash right there and then, and Efendi Ceric was present and I got 50.000 German marks then. They took me to a different building, some other people, they got me a passport and they paid these people to take me to this country where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you find anything out during this meeting that would be of interest to us?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how do I put this? I can just say, as I said to that gentleman of yours, that investigator, I said that then at that moment in 1997, my name was deleted from that list of participants in war. You know that military list? You're not on this military list, you're not in these papers, you're not going to exist any more. It was not done only in my case, it was done in the case of some people who were far greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Efendi Ceric, did he take part in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there, he sat there, and he also got a sum of money out there that he collected through that mosque committee, I'm talking about Alija Izetbegovic and Efendi Ceric. From the two of them, I received 50.000 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was that money intended for?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was intended for - how do it I put this? - so that I no longer -- so that I would no longer exist in Bosnia, go to a different country, work there. You don't know certain things and there you go. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We can redact that but why do we need more detail about this in private session, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just need private session from where he arrived from, how he arrived in Sarajevo. It's a unique way of arriving, that's why perhaps that could be used for decoding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking you what relevance does it have at all, the meeting of this witness with younger Izetbegovic in 2010.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the circumstances involved, Excellency and the people who took part in this and how they treated the witness and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How were you treated in SIPA and what was expected of you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that a bit yesterday. When I came to SIPA to the second floor, in front of Bajro Kulovac and Damir Alagic, that's when I discussed this with Kulovac, why he is talking about these six persons of -- from Skelanci when they did not take part in these killings, and he said, I found evidence, casings, et cetera, and I said, All right, but your people were not killing, and he said, I know better than you, and here are these papers, write this. And I read this piece of paper and what it said was that I was never in Srebrenica from 1992 to 1995. I didn't want to sign that and then I was slapped in the face and kicked, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then Bajro Kulovac and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat from where you said you read this paper -- "... piece of paper and what it said was that I was never in Srebrenica from 1992 to 1995." Please start over again from there. And speak very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came to SIPA with Damir Alagic and Bajro Kulovac from OSA police, I was taken to SIPA to an office. When I arrived in SIPA at the office, first, with Bajro Kulovac I had this discussion as to why six men from Skelanci who were 30 or 40 years old were convicted, although they were not involved in the killings in Kravica. He answered that he had evidence, he found the casings, he found the flesh, the bones and that he found clothes. And I said, All right, you found that as evidence. And these people, these casings that you found, are they with their fingerprints? And he said, You have no right to interfere in that. I am the man in charge and you should sign this paper here and this paper of one page and a half contained my name and surname, confirming that I was not in Srebrenica from 1992 to 1995. I, Judge, did not want to sign that. In the presence of Damir Alagic, Bajro Kulovac slapped me in the face and I fell off the chair and then he managed to kick me in the stomach. How do I put this? Then Damir Alagic said that he should calm down because I came and you know full well where I was and where I came from and that he would take care of all of that. Then I was taken, accompanied by Alagic and Kulovac, to the office of the main director of SIPA, where Damir Alagic, when this man walked in through the door, did not want to talk to this director. He asked for Bosniaks. He didn't want to talk to this man because this man was a Serb. At the time, this man -- well, this other man came, a Muslim, I guess, now was he the deputy director of SIPA, I don't know exactly. This man came and asked me whether I was forced to give a statement at the prosecutor's office in Bijeljina or not. I said -- I just managed to say I was not forced, it's mine. I just wanted to say it was in good faith. Damir Alagic put his hand on my left shoulder and he said that he would take care of this. So from there, I left SIPA and I was in the street for two days and two nights until a lawyer found me and now I don't want to mention his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you the only person who was registered as being killed, or do you know of other cases that people were registered as being killed and who were nevertheless alive like you?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other people like that, Mr. President, Judges, Prosecutors, but these people are abroad and some of them are in the federation to this day. How do I explain this to you? I asked your co-ordinator, as we call him, I asked for a computer, laptop, that we sit down and I can find all of them on Facebook and we can go and see them and have a cup of coffee, but we were not allowed to cross over from Republika Srpska to the federation. So that the Court could see here today that these people are still alive, whereas their parents receive a pension to this day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are any of these people registered in some of the lists that are of interest to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is this list. It was given already in Bijeljina, I think, and it's because of that list that Alagic and Kulovac threatened me that I should not dare speak about that, that's why I fared this way. I would like to see this list here in court, if possible, whether that is the list or another list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that that is what you suffered for the most?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D99586, could that please be shown to the witness in e-court. Could it please not be broadcast? That's probably what it is. Could it please not be broadcast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask something. Can -- can a person ever light a cigarette here in Holland?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hardly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D99586. Do you have the good number? And don't broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D99586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not simply 9586?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Maybe, sorry. [Interpretation] Yes, that's the right number, 9586.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first page of my - how shall I call it? - war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 7. Can you tell us in public session where are these people and how did you come to have these names? What is this list? And then we'll close the session for any additional information.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the list of people who are alive and whose parents receive pensions on account of them being registered as dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you mention in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with any of these people? Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some people who are in Switzerland, there are some who live in the US, some in France. There is this man of yours who lives in Holland. I don't know whether they live in Holland under their own name or under some other name, but if I had my laptop I could get them on Facebook for you and you could talk to them on Skype maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These circled names, except 15 or 16, are they alive? You are satisfied that they are alive? You know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these names that are circled are the people with whom I have had contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this diary under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is because of this list that I had my bones broken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would ask more questions as to the -- this diary, this war diary, when he wrote, and et cetera. Could you carry on. I will ask him. When did you write this, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote this when I was you know where for three and a half years, and through this writing and these documents that I provided to your Office of the Prosecutor here in The Hague of the ICTY who visited me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a Judge, I know nothing about this. I asked when you wrote this. Could you assist us when you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was written while I was -- I don't want to reveal now where I was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who has the original of this --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Who has the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original of this document is in my possession. I don't have it here now but it's in my handwriting and everything, and the Bijeljina prosecutor's office has it. I don't know if it's before this Court, if it's available, if the Court can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're tendering this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 1 and 7, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you could admit into evidence all that you've admitted, I stand by all the documents that I've written. I paid for them with my life. I fought 17 years to sit in this box, to be on this stand, and I am addressing you, the four main people in this Court, to approve my going to the federation and my presence there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a criminal proceedings against Mr. Karadzic. It is for the accused to tender the documents or exhibits and to determine what documents he should tender. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: In short, in my submission, this -- admitting this one page of a document compiled by the witness after the war in the manner of a statement, a diary, a book, a statement, that's what it amounts to, in essence, is admitting part of a prior statement but not in compliance with the procedures that are available under the rules. There has been an effort to admit this witness's statement given to the Defence legal advisers under 92 ter and that application was refused and the witness is called viva voce, and just to admit part of something else that he's compiled to assist in the presentation of his evidence is plainly wrong in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But as a matter of practicality, the witness can read out these -- this list of names and he can say that they are alive, so there is no difference, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, is of course right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what you said seems to go to the weight. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will mark these two pages pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit MFI D4183 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. I have no further questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get some water?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wonder if the witness needs a break maybe. You can ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe if I can just have one cigarette.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing is allowed here. If the International Court cannot give me a break, who can? I remember everything. It's not easy for me. I don't even know what the date is today. Nobody is asking me what I've gone through in my life, in the 1990s. I'm soaked now completely. It's all coming out of me. Let me tell you, Judge, every year, never mind that this is 2013, this may go on with me until the day I die. All that I went through in 1995, on that date or seven days before, I have health problems. I sit down and cry. Sometimes I wanted to kill myself. And nobody, not even your Prosecutor who visited me, did not enable me to come here before, for me to show you what this is all about. I'm asking for a break to have a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We were planning to have a break at 10.30 but we'll have a break now for 15 minutes and resume at ten past. --- Break taken at 9.56 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, we will have another 20 minute break at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, you are here today finally testifying in The Hague, something you have wanted to do for many years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Because you consider yourself to be an important witness, you witnessed, so you believe, many important events during the war; is that right? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You witnessed Muslims killing each other, the ABiH killing Muslims, killing children in Srebrenica, you know that Muslims whose families are claiming benefits because they are dead, you know they are alive, you personally witnessed, so you say, every conspiracy theory that everyone else gets to read about in the press; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you have to ask that of the three women of Srebrenica as well as Sulejman Backovic [as interpreted], a teacher. You should ask them how come they know better what happened in Srebrenica than we who were actually there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Because you know so much, so you say, people want to kill you, they beat you, they put pressure on you, or they ignore you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I was beaten. I've been ignored. A lot of bad things are written about me in the newspapers. A lot of the bad things are known in the public.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 19 and 20, the witness said: You should ask the first three women from the Mothers of Srebrenica, this is an association, the SDA and Sulejman Tihic. This is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You were even captured on tape, so you say, on more than one occasion. We saw a recording yesterday of you apparently in Pale. You told us yesterday there was some footage of you with General Morillon during his speech in Srebrenica in 1993. And let me ask you this: There is one interview, the first interview you had with the Defence legal adviser who is here in court, Goran Petronijevic, your first interview, you said you saw your shoe in footage of Kravica warehouse; is that right? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, there was a print of the shoe, and I asked them to take me there to get that shoe as hard evidence. However, we did not have the time to go there and to fetch the shoe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You have avidly followed The Hague and the state court trials, haven't you? You've watched these trials on television, on the internet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, let me tell you in answer to that, I've watched some the cases. Because I had to work to survive, I didn't have time to sit and watch all the trials. I did it when I had the time to do that. And then I would see a witness talking about Srebrenica here. I found that the hardest thing in my life because those witnesses did not tell the truth as to what they had seen. Their testimonies were biased and what they said was that they were ill treated by the Serbs, and nobody says nor do they dare say that they were treated in Srebrenica from 1992 to 1993, that we were all tortured by the other locals of Srebrenica, by Naser and his men. Who is it who came to this courtroom and said that? If you want me to -- if you want to co-operate with me and the Prosecutor's office want to co-operate with me, I can bring 50 people who would tell you the same thing as I'm saying. They are afraid to say the same thing in Bosnia because they are ill treated, they are provoked, they are threatened and everything else, and people have to suffer. They are hungry, they are thirsty, and they are afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you tell us you can bring 50 people who would give some evidence or other. You have taken it upon yourself to research these cases, haven't you? You've spoken to people who you consider to be witnesses yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you can't understand me, but please try. Listen carefully. I'm going to tell you in very short lines. Since 2003 I have suffered, when -- I suffered when I was in that country where I lived from 2003 to 2007. There was a search warrant for me when Naser Oric was here in 2003 and 2004 because he was afraid that I would hide and he didn't want me to come here while he was still here. And Madam, at that time --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm interrupting you, my apologies, but I'm interrupting you. I asked you a question, I'd like you to answer it, please. You have taken it upon yourself to research these cases, haven't you? Can you answer that question for me?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it upon me because I've been fighting to come here since 1996. The authorities would not allow me to do that. The Sarajevo police arrested me, they beat me, the Sarajevo SDA fabricated all the evidence against me, so I did not manage to come here. Many people are familiar with my case. They know what has happened to me and as a result of that, they themselves are afraid to come here and talk to you. Now I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You -- I don't want to mention where you were but you were in a place over the last few years, we talked about it in private session, when you were there, this was your preoccupation, wasn't it? Preoccupation was researching these cases?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. I'm not you. It is not up to me to research anything. No, Madam. I was free in that place, I was not ill treated, I was not forced to do anything. I sat down and I wrote about my case, Madam. I wrote to the President of Republika Srpska, to Rajko Kuzmanovic. I wrote to Miro Dodik [as interpreted] who is in office now. I wanted to take them to the sector of Srebrenica. I wanted to take them to a grave -- graves and nobody was interested in doing that in Republika Srpska. How would you feel knowing that you have written to somebody, imploring with them to be taken to the grave to excavate your fellow Muslims [as interpreted] from the grave and at the same time you're watching on television and Rajko Dokmanovic [as interpreted] doesn't want to help you. How would you feel? And those people, that woman, they were all killed right in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 8, "to excavate your fellow Serbs from the grave," not "fellow Muslims."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did mention the Serbs, not the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on line 9, the family name is "Kuzmanovic," not "Dokmanovic."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You followed closely, didn't you, the trial of the members of the Special Police Brigade who were indicted for the Kravica warehouse killings at the state court?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. I saw their photos in newspapers, and as soon as I saw their photos and I recognised my school colleague, I immediately asked from the prison warden to invite somebody from the Prosecutor's office, I wanted to tell them that those lads were not there. Bajro Kulovac then came and threatened me not to talk about that any more. That was my first encounters with Bajro Kulovac in the prison, when I was in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. I realise now that prison was mentioned in open session. So I can say I've been talking about the period when you were in prison, when you were following these trials. Let me just ask you this: You have been desperate, haven't you, desperate, to come and testify here as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fought for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Objection overruled. Can we go back -- go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had an objection. Madam Pack repeats in her question that the witness followed those trials from prison. She makes it look like the witness confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, when were you looking at photos in newspapers and watching the television and seeing the footage that you've been talking about related to The Hague proceedings and the state court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be asked not to mention the name of the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I was in prison. In 2003 I was not in prison. I could have been here. Your Prosecutor from here paid me a visit at that time. And there was another man from Srebrenica who testified here, but I'll talk about that in private session. You have his video-clip, you have his testimony, and he was the first to ever mention that -- my name before the Prosecutor who had brought him from that country. And when he visited me, he listened to that conversation and ever since I've had problems. And Naser Oric was here at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to just show you a part of your first interview with the accused's lawyer, Goran Petronijevic and Milomir Savcic, his chief investigator, this is while you were in prison in February 2010.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 25759. And I'd like to go, please, in the English, to page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No broadcast, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast. I'm grateful to Dr. Karadzic. English page 198, B/C/S page 193.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is at the end of your interview, relatively near the end of your interview. It's line 31 down in the English and I'll read it out and you can read the corresponding B/C/S. You say -- talking about giving evidence, you say: There is no problem, if you want tomorrow or the day after, in five in 10 days, come again, we shall sit down, but please know so from now on I only ask for protection. Do you see where I'm reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Serbian page is not --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry, it's the next page in the B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: See where it begins? It's the first -- second paragraph with your initials. So I'm starting there. And then I read on: So from today on I only ask for protection, that nothing would be known about me until my turn to testify comes. Would that be defence of Karadzic or some other issues only to say the Serbs did not take Srebrenica heroically and they did not take that either, but Srebrenica was sold for money, no one has to convince me, we, the army, have abandoned it so they could come in on that terrain. Question: You are worried about your safety? Answer: I'm worried about my safety. From here I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies. Next page. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So it's just going on to the large paragraph: I'm worried about my safety. From here I want only that the trip would be secured for me. So when I would go to testify from here, so I get out in March from here, I want a car to be waiting for me and to take me to testify, et cetera. It goes on. And you go on to say: As people would say, not to see the territory of the former Yugoslavia, so it could only be Holland, The Hague, and the stand. In quotes, "Take the stand, do you claim this?" I do, bring me that man, come here, do you think that this was here? It was, where did you do this? Here and here. And I'm running away from Sarajevo, to tell you the truth, as there would be violence down there as down for me it would be -- Answer: Are you ready -- Question: Are you ready to eventually testify in The Hague about all this what we talked about? Answer: Could we go now immediately? Question: Well, we cannot because the procedure is such. Answer: Let me say --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Serbian new page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Answer: Let me say I understand but it could be now, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow. I'm now here, but that also my condition would be met. I am not asking to take the stand as I see on TV some trials in The Hague. There is a link, some other voices. Face to face, would it be Ratko Mladic? Would it be, for example, Seselj? Would it be Karadzic? Over the next page. Would it be Naser Oric? Would it be Smajo Mandzic? Would it be Zulfo Tursun, face to face? What I went through, what I saw, I do not fear God. I do not fear to look you here into the eye. I do not fear any court. Does that capture -- does that recall well, Witness, your enthusiasm to testify here in The Hague? It was an exciting prospect for you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, what it says here, I stand by it. I stood by it when we talked to the person whose name I should now mention or perhaps not. When I provided this statement, I stood by every word. And then when I was released, 22 days later, I was kidnapped, I was beaten, my bones were broken, I barely survived and got to the civilian police, to the person who finally protected me in my town, in the place where I was born. I spent 22 days there under the protection of the civilian police because when I provided this statement and when I mentioned the names of all those people that you have just read out, ever since then I've had problems with people in the place where I was born. And - how shall I put it? - in the entire federation, I will always have problem with the whole world because of that. Let me tell you, I'm looking you in the eye, Madam, we have a problem in this country where I come from. They are asking after me. People are -- come to me at all costs. They are trying to get in touch with me. If they only knew my address, they would finish me off because I'm the only person in this courtroom that sacrificed my own life and whatever I have now I fought for it. I just implored with the people who have a link to you, to the International Criminal Tribunal, to bring me here as soon as possible. I wanted to come at the moment when I provided that statement. On the 12th March 2010, when I was released, in the last moments people came in two jeeps and they were supposed to fetch me and take me to an unknown destination. I have witnesses for that. I have proof of that. I have documents about those people who were waiting for me. And in the last ten seconds, I managed to get -- to avoid getting into the car. Those people were from the federation, from Sarajevo. And they told me that later, only later did I learn about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, now would be an appropriate time, a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 20 minutes, and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we go briefly into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to read on the first page what this report says in relation to you, and, as I've said, some of it isn't legible but in the larger second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will not broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking just for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. We are now in open session. Shall we go back to private session to discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm just going to read out to you a part of what was written about you in this report. So let me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just ask: These documents are not being broadcast; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are not broadcasting this document at all. Rest assured.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So back to the document. I'm going to read an extract which won't identify you. On page 2, please, of the B/C/S and English -- could we go to page 2 of the B/C/S. Thank you. Now I'm just going to read an extract about halfway down the page: "Intellectual abilities of" you "are limited. They are at the level of physiological dullness. This is an immature, neurotic and passively dependent personality." And then we just go down. The next paragraph begins again, "Intellectual abilities," and details the category of physiological dullness. And then says: "Information acquired, details certain tests, indicates that this is a non-integrated and emotionally immature person who has severe issues with interpersonal communication, view of parent figures, as well as views on primary and other family." And so it goes on, and it repeats those findings in the conclusion at the following page in the B/C/S. Do you remember those findings being made in relation to you? Don't need to say when or where.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you after that that I am seeing this paper for the first time. I only have the judgement. I only have seen the judgement from 1996. They never gave me this paper and I don't know who wrote this because during the retrial in 2008-2009, if that is the same man, then I don't know what to say because during the retrial he defended me and he described all that had happened to me he. But if it is the man from Banja Luka, from 1996, then that man did say awful things about me, only to get me sentenced, and I had problems with psychiatrists because one of them was telling the truth and the other one wasn't. And nobody ever showed this to me before you. Somebody should bring this man to court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I would ask for this document to be admitted, please, perhaps all three pages is better than just this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we object, Mr. President. There hasn't been -- the witness hasn't confirmed, first of all, the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document. I think it's also a very limited probative value, if there were some traits that would go to falsehoods, that might be relevant, but intellectual abilities marginally relevant to credibility. So number 1, we don't believable that the document -- the foundation has been laid through this witness for the admission of the document; and, number 2, even if there were such a foundation, we think that the probative value is outweighed by any prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Whilst the witness might not have confirmed this document, I -- he has broadly confirmed the fact of having been examined in this period by psychiatrists. I don't want to go into too much detail. But he certainly has confirmed that whilst he might not remember the specific content of this, he certainly confirmed a sufficient -- provided a sufficient basis for admission of this document and it's a matter for you to consider the weight you attach to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, is there any contest as to the provenance of this document as opposed to the acceptance of its clinical findings?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we don't have any information one way or the other on it. All we can see is on the face of the document, the very same things that you could see. So we can't tell you that, yes, we dispute the provenance or we have some information that calls the provenance into question. But at the same time, we don't know that there is correct provenance to this document so we are basically in the same position that you are on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The other issue is this: You mention or submitted that the probative value is outweighed by prejudice. Is this really a document where prejudice arises?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it depends on how you view somebody being called dull and, you know, not having very much intelligence. There is some prejudice to that, I think. It doesn't really go to whether the witness ought to be believed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Without being facile about it, Mr. Robinson, one can imagine an irate teacher in school calling a student dull. They may not like it very much, but it's not really prejudicial. It may be mildly abusive as far as the pupil is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, we would like very much to hear you reply to Mr. Robinson. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the topic of provenance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On that topic, I have what I would urge you to consider is the first page of this document, which you've seen which identifies the provenance of this report very clearly. It passes the report on to another party. I'm not sure whether we should have dealt with it in private session. You can see the contents of the first page. We can perhaps go back to it. It says: This is the report that was taken on this date, and we now hereby forward it to you. So, in my submission, there couldn't possibly be an issue about the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Could you also address the Court on whether you think this is one of those classes of documents which raises the probative against prejudicial balance?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I -- I don't think it does. This is a -- this is a document which is being used to offer, in my submission, insights into this witness, and the issue of probative versus prejudicial, in my submission, doesn't arise. It's not so prejudicial that it shouldn't be admitted. It's not so probative for this to be a question that you really need to consider. It simply goes to offering insight into this witness, into his motivations, into his capacity, perhaps, to be manipulated. But that is, in my submission, what is to be offered by this document, and that's why I read it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it. All the issues go to the weight. We will assign a number for this but we will put it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6559 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say a word, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not at this time, Mr. Witness. Ms. Pack will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We are moving on, Witness. You have written to the Prosecutor's office, we've seen, in Sarajevo urging them to take you seriously as a witness and a victim of genocide, haven't you? We saw the letter that you sent them, yesterday?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's return to the letter we saw yesterday. It was admitted in evidence as D04182.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Shouldn't be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to raise it with you, but, Ms. Pack, I take it you're not going to spend more time than Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour. Certainly I shouldn't be anywhere near that time. I think we are waiting for this document to come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just read out the first paragraph. This is while you were in prison in 2008. And you say: I am requesting the esteemed state prosecutor's office, et cetera, an invitation to testify in the matter of the horrific events, mainly war crimes, for which I could prove to be an extremely important or even key witness. Those are very extreme cases for my personal knowledge which I don't want to detail in this request. And then you request the esteemed prosecutor's office to invite you urgently in your office in Sarajevo so I can state exact information which is important for this state as well as the Prosecution in The Hague. Then you say: I am a witness and a victim of genocide and mass destruction of people who died in horrific events in the period 1993 to 1995: "Dear gentlemen, I know exact dates and executors of the serious crimes committed against the innocent civilian population." It goes on to the passage that Dr. Karadzic read out in court yesterday. It's right, isn't it, Witness, that you were desperate to be interviewed by the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted that, and I said that in my statement as well. I wanted that. And this is the letter which I wrote when Bajro Kulovac visited me for the first time, when I was threatened and when I started telling about what Naser had done. Then he took me to the bathroom and told me that I was not to talk about either Naser or Zulfo Tursun. And then my problems escalated. That was my first encounter with Bajro Kulovac and then my second encounter with him was in 2010.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just clarify because I'm a little confused. You say, do you now, that when you were first visited by Bajro Kulovac, that's whilst you were in prison, you were threatened --

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And taken to the bathroom, yes?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was the duty policeman who knew about that and then the Republika Srpska and then the prison where I was, and you can see the address where I was. The entire prison and everybody jumped their feet to defend me and protect me because people knew what would happen to me, because I did not want to do what Bajro Kulovac wanted me to do. I wanted to come on TV to publicly say what Bajro Kulovac and the prosecutor's office in the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina were doing. And at that time, I was prevented from saying what Naser Oric and the other commanders had done. And ever since then my life has been endangered, and if you will allow me to tell the name of the person who was convicted for war crimes and sentenced to 16 years, the other to 30 years, none of them were there, and people were going to liquidate me because of those papers. The entire administration of the prison knew who was prepared to kill me, and if they had not stood up to defend me I would have been killed and I would not be able to testify here today. I can tell you the names of those people who saved me. I don't see a problem in that, just say the word, and this is the message that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This story you're telling us now, this story about being harassed, it seems, during an interview that was conducted in prison, right, that's the story you're telling us today, yes?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, when the prosecution arrived in the prison to talk to me, when I started telling them my story about how things had happened, then Bajro Kulovac, the prosecutor who worked for the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, took me to the corridor, I asked him to go to the bathroom and a policeman who was on duty in the prison was behind us and he told me, when it comes to Naser, Zulfo, and others, don't tell me anything about them. And ever since then, Madam, I've had problems. When we completed that conversation, he went to Sarajevo. A message came to that prison where I was, that I would not come out of that prison alive because there are Muslims there who had been sentenced to 20 years, to ten years, I don't know whether they had been bribed to do things or what, but the word came from outside that I had to be killed. One of the convicts heard about that and informed the prison administration what would happen to me when I was taken out to lunch, and the police were waiting for us to come to lunch. One of the convicts was in front of me, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) and I was supposed to be in the prosecutor's office in Sarajevo and I was supposed to testify about those people in Skelanci but nobody wanted to invite me as a witness. They believed a false witness, Enver Svico [phoen], and he told them the story that was the story of my life and not his life. He lied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You interrupted the interpreters, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Line 5, or at least the end of line 5, should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to invite you as a witness?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this encounter. You gave a very long statement to the SIPA investigators who came to interview you in prison in May 2008. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you're talking about the arrival of Bajro Kulovac, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. And you signed, or perhaps you don't remember, we can look at it in a moment, but you signed your name on every single page of that statement and at the end of it, yes? Remember that?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. But, Madam, I was never invited to testify. Why I wasn't? Because they did not want to invite me to Sarajevo. It is easier to convict somebody on false evidence. And after I gave my statement, when Bajro Kulovac returned to Sarajevo and when Naser and everybody else learned of what would happen, ever since then my life has been in danger. I'm not afraid of that statement before you or before God. You can show it to whoever. You can play it for the entire world. There were perhaps three or four CDs altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, can we just clarify. This statement that you gave, a number of pages which you signed, you gave that statement before or after you were taken to the bathroom by Bajro Kulovac, as you've described moments ago? I would just like to clarify with you what happened in that encounter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could it be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before, before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: -- shown to the witness so to avoid any confusion?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We'll get there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Before we look at your statement I want to ask you about one thing that you spoke about this morning and yesterday. And I want to deal with this carefully because I think it's upsetting for you to deal with it. It's 1992, in Bratunac. You told us yesterday, transcript T 44745, you told us that your mother and son stayed when you were taken off and held at the location in Bratunac you described while you were taken to the stadium. Now, is that right? Is it right that after you were taken off to the stadium, you never saw your son and your mother again after that moment in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, may I start? Let me answer. When I was taken out of the cellar of my house, together with four or five other people, my mother and my son stayed behind in the house, on the first floor. When we were taken out of that basement, when we -- and when we were taken to the gate, do you want the name of those people?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We don't need names.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they took us to the gate, it was only then that my mother came out of the house carrying my first son. I was the last in the column. We were being taken to the football pitch. And I didn't manage to see who opened fire. There were two men. I didn't have the time to turn around to see who had killed them because when I was turning my head to see who had fired the shots, I could only see them falling down. So much for me on that. And as for my mother and my son, another prosecutor's office will investigate that because I can see that you here do not want to hear the names of those people. They were found last year and they were buried. First they were exhumed and then they were reburied. You can go to Bratunac and you can see it for yourself. And don't ask me about that, about my family, about relatives. When you received those papers, why didn't you come looking for me? Why didn't you come and ask who that man was? Where is he? Why didn't you look for me? You and this Tribunal. You in Sarajevo, when you found the papers, why didn't you say we need to talk to this man? Let's see where he is. And the things that were imputed on me that I had been convicted for the killing of one Muslim, it was down to the politics, Bosko Djukic, did that, Naser did that, to make sure that I did not come out of the prison alive. Bring them here. I want to look them in the face. I want to see all the documents. I want to say to the Judges here all the documents that you are going to show to me here today, no problem at all. I can sit here for the whole day today or for the entire month. Show me all the documents. I want to see these people who authored those documents face to face. I want them all to sit here like these people are sitting here today. I want to look him in the eye.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to 65 ter 25520.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is the witness examination record, the record of your interview with SIPA. Can we have this not broadcast, please. Now, I'm just going to read out the content of the first page while we are waiting for it to come up. It's the title page. It's an interview -- a witness examination record and it's dated the 16th of May, 2008. And you are being interviewed by two SIPA investigators - you see it now, it's come up - Bajro Kulovac and Zarko Kalem. And you see your name there? Can you see all that there on the first page?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And if we just go a few pages on, just to get a sense of this document -- well, you can see, first of all, your signature is at the bottom of this first page; right?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And you remember signing every page of this document and being warned --

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you that I signed everything, and as for this other gentleman, SIPA investigator Zarko Kalem, is he a fat guy? If he is then bring him here to the courtroom, whenever you want, I'll be here and I will listen to him telling you what was happening to us. I personally invite this man, Zarko Kalem, to come here and tell you what happened, how I made sure to escape the destiny that had awaited me and I did it already in that bathroom. I managed to save myself. He can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So it's the Zarko Kalem, is it, who was in the bathroom with you? What do you say he did in the bathroom? This is in May 2008 when he interviewed you.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, Bajro Kulovac was with me in the bathroom, and if this man Zarko Kalem, is a fat guy, he will know when I returned from the bathroom, that I started shouting and screaming and he knows what the police officer told him when I had come out of the bathroom. I'm inviting this man to tell you. And that policeman who escorted me, he returned and when I said to that guy, Zarko, and that Prosecutor was there and that recording clerk who were recording on CD what I was saying, and when he was told what had happened, from then on I never wanted to talk to them again. And this guy, the fat Zarko Kalem, the investigator, he said that he would write a complaint about the conduct of his colleague towards me. So you invite him and I am inviting also the police officer, the sergeant, as a witness and I don't want to discuss this document at all. This document should have been discussed in Sarajevo. I should have been invited as a witness instead of being threatened with murder while at the same time an innocent man is being on trial. And because of that in 2010, I was beaten up because I did not want to overlook this. I gave a statement to that effect. I asked them, why did you call Skelanci.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's just try and deal with this occasion, and not go on to other matters so we are dealing with this occasion. You write this long statement which you sign at some point, take a long -- you write this long statement, you have this long interview, rather, you then go to the

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the prison, in the presence of the police sergeant. And when I was supposed to testify, nobody called me because they realised that I would give them all the details. And if you think that I am a psychopath or something of that kind, I'm inviting you to put me on a lie detector and show me documents because I had been through all of that for three years, and before all of you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's fine --

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't make me look like a fool. I'm telling you this was a fabricated process. Bajro Kulovac and Damir Alagic fabricated all that and the other guy, what's his face, Batko Izetbegovic. Madam, my life was at stake. I was threatened for having spoken about all the cases, about that diary. I was threatened with liquidation. I was threatened that I would never leave the prison alive. People came to me from SIPA, all the Gods came to fetch me so I wouldn't appear here. Damir Alagic called me on the telephone and threaten on the telephone. He told me that I was looked for by The Hague and if -- he told me don't talk to them before I arrived. I don't want to discuss this. I will discuss this only when I see Bajro Kulovac and others. This fell through and because of that I had to sign the paper that I talked about because they forced me to sign a paper at the SIPA that I was never in Srebrenica. I don't want to discuss this at all. When I see these people here then I can talk to them eye to eye. Eyeball to eyeball, can I talk to them. I don't want to discuss these documents before I see these people before this International Tribunal, the most famous Tribunal in the world for seeking the truth. They want to make money. That's all they are after. They are fighting for the votes. And my people are starved even more than during the war. My people are more afraid. Muslims, Croats and Serbs are more afraid now than they were during the war. I'm talking on behalf of everybody. I want this document to be tendered and admitted into my defence. I want this Trial Chamber to call all these people, Damir Alagic, Kulovac. And that Alagic called me on the telephone in 2010. He says: The Hague is after you, if they find you, you don't tell them anything before I arrive, I will do everything. And he said that he sent some papers here, and he says: You no longer exist in this story. I saved your life once and that's it. And that was when Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hold on. You stop threatening me. My life is at stake, not yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, not at all. Ms. Pack was never threatening you at all. Please listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say, Judge, that she was threatening me. I was threatened because of the documents that she is now showing me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The transcript is wrong. The transcript is wrong. The witness did not say that the Prosecutor is threatening him. He says that he has been threatened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of these papers, my life is at stake, and now you're showing me these papers from the time when they were done in 2008, 2009. Why didn't you ask me to come when these papers were drafted? Why didn't you look for those people who took that statement? Why didn't you invite me here? I wanted to look you in the face then and tell you what I know like I'm telling you now. Why didn't you ask me to come then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. Mr. Witness, I stopped you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to talk to you any more. Can I get some water?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's difficult, Witness, isn't it, when you've been caught in a lie; right? It's difficult not to lose your temper.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody, Madam, caught me in a lie here because I'm not afraid of you or this Court when I'm telling the truth. It's difficult for you because you're unable to bring this Kulovac and this Zarko people before this Court to tell you what really happened. And I can bring you the whole prison administration and the police sergeant who was on duty then and two more people to testify what I was told in that prison and how I was threatened. I have five witnesses and you bring me this Zarko Kalem and Bajro Kulovac to confront me. And I can bring five more witnesses to confirm what had been done to me. I didn't come here, Madam, to lie, that's one. And I'm not afraid of that. I was telling the truth. And while I was interrogated and while I went in the field, I passed everything, I passed the lie detector test and I passed everything and all the documents in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that Sarajevo writes, I don't give a damn about it until I see those people from Sarajevo here. What Bajro Kulovac, what Damir Alagic writes, this Bakir Izetbegovic, until I see them sitting on that bench over there, then I can bring my own witnesses to testify what they had done with my life. The rest I will not discuss until that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We will get this over much quicker if you answer more coherently and less lengthily. Now, let me just ask you: What do you say happened in the bathroom at the prison just after your interview when you signed this interview? What do you say happened? And just tell us in a sentence. Don't need to give us -- go into anything else.

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, what happened is that I should not dare speak about Kravica or Srebrenica at all for fear of Bajro Kulovac. I was told that by Bajro Kulovac in the presence of the police sergeant, and when I returned inside with the police sergeant, this Zarko Kalem, his name is written here, I was shouting, I was screaming, Why are you threatening me, et cetera, et cetera, and then I left the office. And the news of that incident reached the deputy minister of Republika Srpska, who is being attacked because Bajro Kulovac and Damir Alagic were telling him that I'm crazy. They showed a programme, 60 minutes on the BHTV. Damir Alagic appeared in that TV show saying that I'm crazy, that I don't know what I'm talking about, et cetera. That's why I don't want to discuss any papers from Sarajevo until I am able to confront these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Were you hit, were you beaten, by the investigator when you were in the bathroom?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the bathroom I was told only that, it was in 2010 that this man beat me up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You see, it's pure fantasy, isn't it, Witness, pure fantasy, what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: KW12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's fantasy bring those people here to confront me, if I'm fantasising.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
